newsitem.title: HUNGARY: EU aspirants await summit to start enlargement.
newsitem.headline: EU aspirants await summit to start enlargement.

text.p: As the European Union headed into its Amsterdam summit on Monday, countries poised to become new members hoped that EU squabbles over monetary union would not further delay the start of enlargement talks.

"We hope that after Amsterdam the countdown will start and early next year the accession negotiations will begin," said Ferenc Somogyi, state secretary for integration in Hungary, widely seen as among the candidates for first-round entry.
The two-day Amsterdam summit was originally called to wrap up a months-long EU inter-governmental conference (IGC) whose job was to make reforms needed to expand the 15-nation bloc.

That agenda may be overshadowed by a Franco-German rift over a stability pact, a cornerstone of the monetary union planned for 1999, agreed in Dublin last year and now due for ratification in Amsterdam.

But applicant countries hoped the EU would stick to a timetable of publishing on July 16 recommendations concerning the various candidates' readiness to join the world's biggest and richest club of democracies. Enlargement talks could then begin.
"There is nothing (from the IGC) which would be against our expectations," Somogyi told Reuters in an interview.
Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia Lithuania, Latvia, Bulgaria and Romania have applied for EU membership. Cyprus also hopes to join.
But as in the case of NATO enlargement, not all EU applicants have equal chances of joining in the first round or possibly any time soon, officials and analysts caution.

Romania, for example, could wind up a two-time loser. The United States said pointedly last week it wants only three new members in NATO -- Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland -- although France and Germany favoured Romania and Slovenia too.
Romanian centrists who ousted ex-communists last November have been pressing for early membership of NATO, figuring the admission requirements were easier to fulfil than for the EU.
"Our fundamental option for building democratic structures that underpin a market economy involve a longer time span," Romania's European Integration Minister Alexandru Herlea said.
John Roper, associate fellow at Chatham House of the Royal Institute of International Affairs in London, agreed it was impractical to admit countries to the EU before they are ready.
"These organisations don't exist to be good news for Romania," Roper said. "They are good news for existing members and for members coming in and this isn't being beastly to Romania.
"It is saying objectively you haven't got the structures which make it possible for you to operate on a common basis and it would be to your disadvantage to come in too soon."
But Jorgen Mortensen, an analyst with the Centre for European Studies in Brussels, argued for rapid enlargement, saying the problems may not be as great as people fear.

"We are already for most of these countries pulling towards the end of the first five-year period (of association agreements) and there would be rather little protection of their domestic industries in the next five years," he said.

"So I would argue that comprehensive enlargement would be a better approach than an extended period of free-trade agreements with countries already participating quite strongly in economic integration."
Even countries which are further along and are deemed prime EU material, like Hungary, the Czech Republic ,and Poland, face a tough job to meet EU admission requirements

Poland has won praise for macroeconomic achievements but a forthcoming EU assessment of preparations for membership is expected to harshly criticise trade protectionism, slow privatisation and failure to launch many vital reforms.

The EU is also concerned about Poland's outmoded agriculture. Analysts say the number of farms would have to be cut to some 800,000 from more than two million if Poland is to be embraced by the EU's Common Agricultural Policy.

"Trade protectionism, failure to dismantle some state-owned monopolies, and a passive attitude to reforming the state sector and agriculture are likely to be negatively assessed in the EU avis (opinion)," said Krystyna Gawlikowska-Fueckel, an analyst of the IBnGR think-tank.

Among the ex-Soviet Baltic states, Estonia is widely viewed as having made the greatest strides towards reforming its economy, privatising state companies and bringing its legislation into line with EU rules. But Estonia also admits it has a long way to go, especially in legislative matters.
"We know we have much work ahead of us but the government and parliament are certain they are able to accomplish this work," Foreign Minister Toomas Ilves told parliament last week.
Hungary's Somogyi said he believed whatever hurdles remain, enlargement will go ahead.
"The (Amsterdam summit) is not going to be a sensational turning point," he said. "The process with ups and downs that has been going on has become irreversible and is unchangeable
